lines.text:
A Day in the Computer Lab

The computer lab at Park Lane School opens at eight o'clock every morning. There are twenty desktop computers on long desks, and each one has a monitor, a keyboard, and a mouse. Some students prefer to bring their own laptop and connect it to the school's Wi-Fi router instead.

When students arrive, they log in with their username and password. The operating system loads, and familiar icons appear on the screen. Most students open a browser first and use a search engine to find information for their homework. They click on links, open new tabs, and scroll through web pages. Some students open files from a folder on the desktop or from cloud storage.

Mr Karim, the IT teacher, helps students who have problems. 'My cursor is not moving,' says one student. Mr Karim checks the mouse and the mouse pad. Another student cannot find a file. 'Did you save it?' asks Mr Karim. 'Always save your work before you log out.'

In the corner of the room, there is a printer and a scanner. Students can print their essays or scan documents. A USB drive and an external hard drive sit on the shelf for students who need extra storage. Near the door, there is a power strip and a surge protector, which keep the equipment safe.

At the end of the lesson, students save their files, close all windows, and log out. They put their headsets back on the hooks and push their chairs under the desks. The computer lab is quiet again, waiting for the next class.

The lab also has useful accessories. A charger and a USB cable sit in the supply box. A docking station connects a laptop to a larger monitor. A stylus is available for the drawing tablet, and every screen has a screen protector to prevent scratches.

Using a computer well means knowing basic actions: typing, clicking, dragging, copying, pasting, editing, and searching. It also means keeping your password safe, updating your software, and understanding what a firewall does. These are not just school skills — they are life skills.

lines.text: The 'digital divide' refers to the gap between people who have access to technology and those who don't. During the COVID-19 pandemic, this gap became painfully visible — children without computers or reliable internet at home fell behind in their education. Libraries and community centres offering free computer access have become lifelines for many families.

lines.text: Programme vs Program — The Full Picture
lines.name: Programme vs Program — The Full Picture

lines.text: British English: 'programme' for most uses (TV programme, training programme) but 'program' for computing (computer program, programming). American English: 'program' for everything. When you see 'programme' with an -mme ending, it's almost certainly British. Learners often mix these up in academic writing.

lines.text: 'Phishing' (note the spelling — 'ph' not 'f') is a type of online fraud where criminals send fake emails pretending to be from trusted organisations. The word plays on 'fishing' — casting a line and hoping someone bites. Universities, banks, and employers regularly warn against clicking suspicious links. 'Don't take the bait' = don't fall for the trick.

lines.text: In British universities and libraries, there are strong unwritten rules about shared computer use: don't eat or drink near the machines, don't use your phone on loudspeaker, don't watch videos without headphones, and — critically — log out when you leave. Leaving your session open is considered both rude (others can't use the machine) and risky (others can access your files).

lines.text: We 'turn on' or 'switch on' electronic devices. 'Open' is for doors, books, files, and apps — not for starting a machine. 'I opened a file.' 'I turned on the computer.'
